scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

For example, public speaking is uncomfortable for many, but that doesn’t mean we should avoid it entirely. The goal is to **manage discomfort**, not eliminate it by avoiding people. --- ### **What You Could Have Done Differently** 1. **Acknowledge the Feeling, Don’t Reject the Person** - Instead of saying, *"I don’t do friendships with women,"* you could have said: *"I’ve realized I have some irrational feelings about being around women in certain ways, and I don’t want those to affect our working relationship. I’d rather keep things professional and work-focused from now on."* - This is **honest but not dismissive**. It acknowledges the issue without blaming her. 2. **Try to Understand the Feeling** - Instead of rejecting the idea of friendship, you could have asked yourself: - *"Why does this feeling bother me so much?"* - *"Is this about insecurity, or is it about something else?"* - *"Would I feel this way if she were a man?"* (If not, why?) - This is the first step toward **growth**. 3. **Consider Therapy (Even If You Don’t Want To)** - You say you won’t see a psychologist, but that’s like saying you won’t go to the doctor because you don’t want to hear bad news. These feelings are **not just "flaws"**—they’re **patterns** that likely affect your life in ways you’re not even aware of. - Even if you don’t change, **understanding** why you feel this way would help you manage it better. 4. **Reevaluate Your Relationships** - If you’re in a relationship, this behavior is **toxic**. Possessiveness and jealousy are **dealbreakers** for most people. If you can’t tolerate your partner talking to other men, that’s a **red flag**. - If you’re not in a relationship, this avoidance of women is **self-limiting**. You’re missing out on meaningful connections because of your own discomfort. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (Unacceptable)** Your actions were **not just rude—they were self-defeating and potentially harmful**. You rejected a potential friendship (and possibly a coworker’s trust) based on **irrational, uncomfortable feelings** rather than addressing them. That’s not just "AITA"—it’s **a missed opportunity for growth and a failure to engage with reality**. --- ### **What You Can Do Now** 1. **Reflect on why these feelings exist.** Are they about insecurity? Past trauma? Social conditioning? 2. **Try to engage with women in small, controlled ways.** See if the feelings persist or if they’re just discomfort with the unknown. 3. **Consider therapy (even if just for a few sessions).** You don’t have to change—just **understand**. 4. **Stop using "I don’t want to feel this way" as an excuse to avoid people.** Life isn’t about avoiding discomfort—it’s about **managing it**. Would you like help brainstorming ways to approach this with her (if you decide to) or strategies to work on these feelings?
